findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is in one or two plain sentences. That is the page's best service to a first-time visitor.
findings.source: <header> lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: This URL is Athena's own site, yet the title and nearly everything below the header are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets two sentences about it and then a long technical study of something else.
findings.source: Page title: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The page does say why the study exists. But what it shows (reading a project and citing sources) is not the main job Athena claims, which is turning a request into a change to a repository. The page never shows that main job, so the reader has to take it on trust.
findings.source: <header> lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim"

findings.text: The next step is easy to find and linked from the top. However, it is only a link to the repository. The page gives no install command and no one-line way to try Athena.
findings.source: <header>: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section linking https://github.com/doodla/athena

findings.text: The firstmate part opens well: a plain summary, defined terms up front, and a step-by-step walk through one task. A reader who stays can follow the basic flow.
findings.source: "Start here" / "What firstmate is": "Firstmate is a tool for people who direct AI coding agents. It keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a worker..."

findings.text: The transition cards get dense with undefined terms. "Endpoint", "durable record" and "wake" appear in the text, but none of them is in the Glossary.
findings.source: Transition t8: "a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead"

findings.text: Two different states are each called "the final state", which contradicts itself. The States section handles this better by tagging both as "ends the task".
findings.source: Glossary: "done — The final state" and "reopened — The final state of a task whose backlog item was reopened"

findings.text: The finding ids skip f2 and the page does not explain why. Entry f4 also describes the study's own internal history ("A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths"), which means little to a newcomer.
Every claim links to exact file lines at a fixed commit. This is real, checkable evidence for Athena's promise that statements trace back to sources.
findings.source: Claims and sources: e.g. claim c1 linking "AGENTS.md:206-206" at the pinned commit
